title: Bronchiectasis: Chronic Infection, Airway Clearance, and Exacerbation Risk
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is chronic abnormal airway dilation with recurrent infection/inflammation and impaired mucus clearance. Confirm the diagnosis structurally, look for an underlying cause, use airway-clearance and microbiology-informed treatment, and recognize hemoptysis, hypoxemia and rapidly worsening infection as escalation problems.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, daily sputum and intermittent hemoptysis are classic clues.
Exacerbations are clinical deteriorations in cough, sputum amount/purulence, dyspnea, fatigue or systemic symptoms rather than a positive sputum culture alone.
differentiate: Bronchiectasis is not synonymous with COPD; airflow obstruction may coexist but the structural disease, sputum microbiology and airway-clearance needs differ.
Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immune deficiency, aspiration, ABPA and prior severe infection are important cause categories.
assessment: Assess exacerbation frequency, sputum volume/colour, hemoptysis, dyspnea, oxygenation, weight/nutrition, sinus disease, aspiration risk, immune/infection history and prior organisms including Pseudomonas.
Review vaccination, airway-clearance technique, inhaled therapies and antibiotic exposure.
workup: High-resolution CT establishes bronchiectatic airway changes; obtain sputum culture during clinically significant exacerbation when it can change antimicrobial choice.
Use cause-directed immunologic, CF/PCD, ABPA, aspiration or other testing rather than an identical panel for every patient.
management: Teach or reinforce individualized airway-clearance therapy and pulmonary rehabilitation/exercise where appropriate.
Treat exacerbations with syndrome- and culture-informed antibiotics and define a reassessment point; recurrent/high-burden disease should involve respirology/bronchiectasis expertise.
Address the underlying cause and comorbid sinus, reflux/aspiration or obstructive-airway disease when present.
medicationSafety: Avoid indefinite empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics without microbiologic/clinical review because resistance and adverse effects accumulate.
Long-term macrolide or inhaled-antibiotic strategies are specialist-guided and require interaction, QT/hearing and organism-specific safety review.
redFlags: New focal chest pain with pneumothorax concern
Failure of appropriate outpatient exacerbation therapy
counselling: Teach airway-clearance adherence, hydration as appropriate, vaccination, smoking/vaping avoidance and when sputum/respiratory changes require prompt review.
followUp: Track exacerbation frequency, lung function, symptoms, weight and microbiology over time; recurrent Pseudomonas or progressive disease warrants specialty follow-up.
examTrap: Treating every positive sputum culture as an acute infection without asking whether the patient's clinical status has actually changed.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is mucus clearance plus cause control plus microbiology-informed exacerbation management.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Non-CF Bronchiectasis Working Group / current respiratory practice resources

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize Right-Heart Risk and Refer Early
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes, not a diagnosis made from one echocardiographic pressure estimate. Suspect it in otherwise unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart findings, evaluate common secondary causes, and refer confirmed/suspected significant disease to pulmonary-vascular expertise before starting PAH-specific therapy.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pressure, presyncope/syncope, edema and signs of right-ventricular strain raise concern.
Pregnancy in significant pulmonary vascular disease can carry major maternal risk and requires urgent specialist coordination.
differentiate: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is only one pulmonary-hypertension group; left-heart disease, chronic lung/hypoxic disease, chronic thromboembolic disease and multifactorial causes require different treatment.
An echocardiogram estimates probability and right-heart effects; right-heart catheterization defines hemodynamics when definitive classification is needed.
assessment: Assess functional limitation, syncope, edema, oxygenation, JVP/right-heart signs, connective-tissue disease, thromboembolic history, liver/HIV risk, drugs/toxins, sleep-disordered breathing and left-heart/lung disease clues.
workup: Use ECG, chest imaging, echocardiography, pulmonary testing, oxygenation and cause-directed blood tests; evaluate chronic thromboembolic disease when clinically plausible.
Specialist-directed right-heart catheterization is required before many PAH-specific treatment decisions.
management: Treat hypoxemia, volume overload and the underlying cause as appropriate while arranging pulmonary-vascular/cardiology referral.
Do not empirically start PAH-specific vasodilator therapy for an unclassified patient because therapy appropriate for one group can be ineffective or harmful in another.
medicationSafety: Diuretics may relieve right-heart congestion but require renal/electrolyte monitoring.
Pulmonary-vasodilator therapies have class-specific hypotension, hepatic, pregnancy and interaction risks and belong in specialist-guided care.
counselling: Explain that 'high lung pressure' has several causes and treatment depends on defining the hemodynamic group.
Review pregnancy planning, activity tolerance and urgent symptoms with specialist input.
followUp: Ensure closed-loop referral and tracking of functional class, right-heart status, oxygen needs and underlying disease.
examTrap: Starting pulmonary-arterial-hypertension drugs solely because echocardiography estimates an elevated pulmonary pressure.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension must be classified before it is specifically treated.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Pulmonary Vascular Disease Working Group resources

title: Sarcoidosis: Prove the Pattern, Exclude the Mimic, Find Organ Threats
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous diagnosis that requires a compatible clinical/radiographic pattern, exclusion of important mimics and—when tissue is needed—noncaseating granulomatous pathology. The NP priority is identifying organ-threatening cardiac, neurologic, ocular, calcium or advanced pulmonary involvement that changes urgency.
recognize: Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, cough/dyspnea, erythema nodosum, uveitis and constitutional symptoms are common patterns.
Cardiac sarcoidosis can present with conduction disease, ventricular arrhythmia, syncope or cardiomyopathy rather than respiratory symptoms.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma, occupational/environmental granulomatous disease and drug reactions can mimic sarcoidosis.
A granuloma alone is not sarcoidosis; epidemiology, microbiology and the whole organ pattern matter.
assessment: Assess respiratory symptoms, vision/eye pain, palpitations/syncope, neurologic symptoms, skin/joints, calcium/kidney-stone symptoms and occupational/travel/infectious exposures.
workup: Use chest imaging and pulmonary function testing for pulmonary disease; ECG and further cardiac assessment are warranted when cardiac symptoms/findings exist.
Check calcium/renal/hepatic and other organ-directed tests as clinically indicated; biopsy the safest appropriate site when diagnostic tissue is required.
management: Observation is appropriate for some asymptomatic/self-limited disease, whereas significant symptomatic or organ-threatening disease requires corticosteroid or steroid-sparing therapy through specialty pathways.
Urgent specialty/acute-care escalation is required for cardiac, neurologic, vision-threatening or severe hypercalcemic disease.
medicationSafety: Before prolonged immunosuppression, assess infection risk and follow current screening/vaccination guidance.
Do not give empiric prolonged steroids for an undifferentiated granulomatous syndrome before important infections are reasonably excluded.
redFlags: Vision loss or severe ocular inflammation
counselling: Explain the multisystem nature of disease and teach patients to report new visual, cardiac or neurologic symptoms promptly.
followUp: Track the organs involved, lung function/imaging when pulmonary disease is present and therapy toxicity; avoid routine testing unrelated to the patient's known risk pattern.
examTrap: Calling noncaseating granulomas 'sarcoidosis' without considering TB, fungal disease or malignancy.
oneLinePearl: Sarcoidosis is a pattern plus exclusion—not a granuloma label.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory specialty resources

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Protect Lung Function Through Specialized Longitudinal Care
bottomLine: Adult cystic fibrosis is lifelong multisystem disease that belongs in a specialized CF program. Primary/acute-care NPs should recognize pulmonary exacerbation and treatment toxicity, preserve airway-clearance/CFTR-modulator continuity when possible, identify CF-related diabetes/liver/nutrition complications, and coordinate rapidly with the patient's CF team.
recognize: Pulmonary exacerbation can present with increased cough/sputum, dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, appetite/weight change or lung-function decline.
CF complications extend beyond the lungs to pancreatic insufficiency/nutrition, CF-related diabetes, liver disease, bone disease, fertility/pregnancy and mental health.
differentiate: Chronic colonization does not mean every respiratory symptom should be treated with the same antibiotic; prior microbiology and the patient's individualized CF plan matter.
Non-CF bronchiectasis shares airway-clearance concepts but not CFTR-modulator indications or the full CF multisystem pathway.
assessment: Ask baseline lung function, usual organisms, home airway-clearance/inhaled regimen, CFTR modulator, recent antibiotics, oxygen/ventilatory support, nutrition/weight, diabetes and transplant status.
Assess fever, hypoxemia, hemoptysis, dehydration, severe chest pain/pneumothorax signs and treatment adverse effects.
workup: Use sputum culture and chest/laboratory evaluation according to exacerbation severity and the patient's CF plan; compare with prior microbiology and baseline function.
Do not make CFTR-modulator or chronic antimicrobial changes outside current Canadian CF guidance/specialist collaboration.
management: Continue or intensify airway clearance according to the CF plan and involve the CF centre early for suspected exacerbation or admission.
Use antibiotics informed by prior/current organisms, allergies, renal function and prior resistance under the CF protocol.
Manage CFRD, nutrition, liver disease and reproductive care through the multidisciplinary CF pathway.
medicationSafety: CF regimens have major interaction and organ-monitoring considerations, especially CFTR modulators and repeated antimicrobial courses.
Avoid casually substituting, stopping or duplicating chronic inhaled/CFTR therapy during an acute-care encounter without checking the specialized plan.
counselling: Reinforce airway-clearance adherence, individualized infection-control practices, nutrition and CF-team contact for deterioration.
Pregnancy and fertility planning should be coordinated with CF and obstetric specialists because disease status and therapies affect risk.
followUp: Close the loop with the CF centre after any exacerbation, antimicrobial course, hospitalization or new multisystem complication.
examTrap: Treating an adult with CF exactly like routine community-acquired pneumonia without reviewing prior airway microbiology, chronic regimen or CF-centre plan.
oneLinePearl: For CF, the safest NP move is specialized continuity plus rapid recognition of deterioration.
sourceBasis: Cystic Fibrosis Canada — Canadian Guidelines for Cystic Fibrosis Care
Cystic Fibrosis Canada pulmonary exacerbation guidance

title: Mechanical Ventilation: Read the Patient, the Mode, and the Gas Exchange Together
bottomLine: Mechanical ventilation is organ support, not a diagnosis. The NP must distinguish oxygenation from ventilation problems, recognize patient–ventilator distress and urgent complications, and use the respiratory/critical-care team and local protocol for setting changes rather than adjusting one number in isolation.
recognize: FiO2/PEEP primarily influence oxygenation, while minute ventilation and dead-space physiology influence carbon dioxide clearance.
Sudden desaturation/high-pressure alarms can reflect tube obstruction, secretions, bronchospasm, pneumothorax, biting/kinking or worsening lung mechanics.
differentiate: A high peak pressure with relatively unchanged plateau pressure suggests increased airway resistance; elevated plateau pressure suggests reduced respiratory-system compliance when accurately measured.
Hypercapnia does not automatically mean the respiratory rate should simply be increased; evaluate airway, dead space, lung mechanics, patient effort and acid-base context.
assessment: Assess the patient first: airway/tube position, chest rise, breath sounds, oxygen saturation, hemodynamics, mental status/sedation, synchrony and alarm pattern.
Review mode, set vs delivered tidal volume, rate, PEEP, FiO2, pressures and recent ABG/VBG where appropriate.
workup: Use blood gas and imaging when they answer the clinical problem; verify endotracheal-tube position and rapidly evaluate pneumothorax when sudden deterioration suggests it.
Trend oxygenation, ventilation and lung mechanics rather than reacting to one isolated alarm.
management: For sudden ventilator deterioration, stabilize the patient, call respiratory/critical-care support, assess for disconnection/tube problem and use manual ventilation when clinically necessary while the cause is identified.
Use lung-protective ventilation principles for ARDS/appropriate conditions and minimize excessive oxygen exposure once stable according to the active protocol.
Weaning readiness depends on improvement of the underlying problem, hemodynamic stability, oxygenation/ventilatory capacity, mental status and airway protection—not one normal ABG.
medicationSafety: Sedatives/analgesics affect respiratory drive, delirium and hemodynamics; use the lightest effective strategy consistent with safety and the active ICU plan.
Neuromuscular blockade removes visible distress and requires deep sedation/analgesia plus monitored indications.
redFlags: Refractory high pressures or profound hypercapnic/acidemic deterioration
counselling: For families, explain that ventilator numbers are support settings and change with the underlying illness; avoid promising a weaning timeline before physiologic readiness is established.
followUp: Document cause/response to major ventilator events and ensure handoff includes mode, oxygen/PEEP, recent gas exchange, sedation and airway concerns.
examTrap: Treating a ventilator alarm by changing settings before assessing the patient and the airway.
oneLinePearl: On a ventilator, patient first, airway second, machine third—then adjust support to physiology.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Home Mechanical Ventilation guidance

title: Asthma–COPD Overlap: Treat Asthma Risk Without Ignoring Fixed Obstruction
bottomLine: When a patient has persistent airflow obstruction plus convincing asthma features, preserve inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy because asthma biology changes safety. Confirm the phenotype with history and spirometry, treat smoking/exposure and exacerbation risk, and avoid labelling every obstructed smoker as 'overlap'.
recognize: Asthma features include variable symptoms/airflow, earlier onset, atopy and steroid responsiveness; COPD features include persistent post-bronchodilator obstruction, smoking/biomass exposure, emphysema/chronic bronchitis and progressive exertional limitation.
A patient can have both, but the label should follow evidence rather than convenience.
differentiate: Fixed obstruction in long-standing asthma does not automatically equal COPD; emphysema/exposure pattern and longitudinal history matter.
Eosinophilia may support type-2 inflammation but is not by itself a diagnosis of asthma–COPD overlap.
assessment: Confirm inhaler technique/adherence, smoking/vaping/occupational exposure, exacerbations, steroid bursts, atopy, symptom variability, oxygenation and comorbid rhinitis/OSA/reflux.
workup: Use quality spirometry with bronchodilator response and compare prior tests; obtain imaging or additional testing when another cause of obstruction is plausible.
Do not diagnose overlap from symptoms alone without objective airflow assessment when the patient is stable enough for testing.
management: Ensure an ICS-containing regimen when asthma is genuinely part of the phenotype; add long-acting bronchodilator therapy according to symptom/exacerbation burden and current asthma/COPD guidance.
Address smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/activity and written action planning.
Frequent exacerbations or uncertainty about phenotype should prompt respirology review rather than endless empiric inhaler escalation.
medicationSafety: LABA monotherapy is unsafe in asthma and should not be used when asthma is part of the phenotype.
Higher cumulative inhaled/systemic corticosteroid exposure increases candidiasis, bruising, bone, metabolic and infection risks; use the lowest effective evidence-based regimen.
redFlags: Unexpected weight loss/hemoptysis or another alternate diagnosis
counselling: Teach inhaler technique, spacer use when relevant, action-plan triggers and the reason an ICS component remains important when asthma features are present.
followUp: Reassess symptom control, rescue use, exacerbations, spirometry and inhaler technique after treatment change; revisit the diagnosis if the course does not fit.
examTrap: Stopping inhaled corticosteroid and leaving LABA-only therapy in a patient with convincing asthma plus chronic obstruction.
oneLinePearl: If asthma is truly present, protect against asthma risk while treating the fixed obstruction too.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current Asthma Guideline Library
